# Transmission, outbreaks and One Health

> *A pathogen that cannot reach a new host dies with the one it is in. Where do microbes live between
> hosts, how do they travel, and where can transmission be interrupted?*

## The chain of infection {#sec-trans-chain}

Transmission is usually described as a chain of six links. Each link is a point at which the chain
can be broken, so the model is most useful as a checklist for control.

| Link | What it means | Example of breaking it |
|---|---|---|
| **Infectious agent** | The organism itself | Antimicrobial treatment; sterilisation |
| **Reservoir** | Where the organism normally lives and multiplies: people, animals, soil or water | Treating infected people; vector control |
| **Portal of exit** | How it leaves the reservoir: respiratory particles, faeces, blood, skin | Covering coughs; dressing wounds |
| **Mode of transmission** | How it travels (see below) | Hand hygiene; safe water; mosquito control |
| **Portal of entry** | How it enters the next host: mouth, airway, broken skin, mucosa | Gloves; safe injection practice |
| **Susceptible host** | A person who can be infected | Vaccination |

Reservoirs differ in a way that matters for control. An organism whose only reservoir is humans can
in principle be eradicated: smallpox was, and polio is close. An organism with an animal or
environmental reservoir cannot be, because it persists whatever happens in the human population.

A **zoonosis** is an infection transmitted from animals to humans. Around 60% of known human
infectious diseases, and about 75% of emerging ones, originate in animals [@taylor2001risk]. A
**vector** is an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts, usually a mosquito, tick, flea or
louse. A **fomite** is an inanimate object that carries organisms, such as a door handle or a shared
keyboard.

## Routes of transmission {#sec-trans-routes}

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/transmission-sorter.yml"></div>

The respiratory route needs a further note, because its description changed during the COVID-19
pandemic. Exhaled particles span a continuous range of sizes. Large particles fall to the ground
within a short distance; small ones evaporate and stay suspended, so they accumulate in poorly
ventilated rooms and can infect people further away. The older teaching split these into two
categories at a fixed size cut-off, which is now recognised as too rigid [@wang2021airborne]. For
control, distance, duration of exposure and ventilation all matter.

## Measuring how an infection spreads {#sec-trans-measures}

Four quantities describe transmission, and each answers a different question.

| Quantity | Question it answers | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Incubation period** | How long between infection and symptoms? | Sets how long contacts are observed |
| **Infectious period** | When can this person pass it on? | May begin before symptoms, which makes control much harder |
| **Basic reproduction number, R₀** | How many people does one case infect in a fully susceptible population? | A property of the organism *and* of the population |
| **Effective reproduction number, R** | How many does one case infect now, given immunity and control measures? | Above 1, cases grow; below 1, the outbreak shrinks |

Because R falls as immunity rises, there is a level of immunity above which an outbreak cannot sustain
itself. This **herd immunity threshold** is 1 − 1/R₀. For an organism with an R₀ of 2 it is 50%; for
a highly transmissible one with an R₀ of 12 it is above 90%, which is why measles needs such high
vaccination coverage.

<div data-island="epidemic-sim" data-src="/diagrams/epidemic-sim.yml"></div>

The model shows three general features. The outbreak ends while susceptible people remain, because
transmission falls below replacement before everyone has been infected. Reducing transmission both
lowers the peak and delays it, which is the reasoning behind measures intended to keep demand within
hospital capacity. And a small change in R₀ makes a large difference to the final number infected,
because the effect compounds with each generation of cases.

## Investigating an outbreak {#sec-trans-outbreak}

An **outbreak** is more cases of a disease than expected in a given place and time. **Endemic** means
constantly present in a population; an **epidemic** is a sharp rise above that baseline; a **pandemic**
is an epidemic across many countries.

Investigation follows a standard sequence:

1. Confirm that the cases are real, and define what counts as a case.
2. Describe the cases by person, place and time.
3. Use that description to form a hypothesis about the source.
4. Test the hypothesis by comparing exposures between people who became ill and people who did not.
5. Act to interrupt transmission, without waiting for the investigation to be complete.

The shape of an **epidemic curve**, a plot of cases against time of onset, carries information. Cases
that cluster within one incubation period suggest a single shared exposure; the wedding lunch case in
[*Gram-positive cocci*](../microbes/gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-case) is an example. Cases spread
over successive incubation periods, each wave larger than the last, suggest spread from person to
person.

## Hand hygiene: the evidence came first {#sec-trans-semmelweis}

In the Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s, two maternity clinics had very different death rates from
**puerperal fever**, infection after childbirth. In the clinic staffed by medical students, who came to
deliveries from the autopsy room, mortality ran several times higher than in the midwives' clinic
[@semmelweis1861]. Ignaz Semmelweis reasoned that something was being carried on hands from the dead
to the living, and required staff to wash their hands in chlorinated lime. Deaths fell sharply.

He could not say what was being carried, since germ theory was decades away, and his colleagues
largely rejected the finding. The episode shows that an interruptible route is enough to act on, the
same lesson as John Snow's investigation in the case at the end of this chapter. It is also why hand
hygiene remains the single most effective measure against healthcare-associated infection.

## One Health {#sec-trans-onehealth}

**One Health** is the principle that human, animal and environmental health are interdependent, and
that infections are best understood and controlled across all three. The connections are practical:

- Most emerging infections come from animals, so surveillance in animals gives earlier warning.
- Antimicrobials used in animals select resistant bacteria that reach people through food, water and
  direct contact.
- Changes in land use, climate and travel alter where vectors can live and which animals humans meet.

Singapore applies the approach in several ways. Dengue control acts on the vector, including the
release of male mosquitoes carrying *Wolbachia* ([*The microbial
world*](microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-harmless)). Surveillance of hand, foot and mouth disease covers
childcare centres, where asymptomatic carriage is common. The 1999 outbreak of Nipah virus infection
was traced to pigs imported from Malaysia and was controlled by acting on the animal side. Melioidosis
is acquired from soil and surface water, and cases rise after heavy rain ([*Microbes and their
hosts*](host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-case)).
